title: The Speed-Accuracy-Energy Pareto Frontier in Deliberative Biological Nervous Systems and Synthetic Reasoning Models
plain_title: Thinking longer costs energy, in brains and AI
thesis: Brains and AI reasoning models both cut their mistakes by thinking longer, and both pay for it in time and energy along one shared trade-off curve.
summary: The paper argues that fast reflexes (a fly steadying itself in 5 ms) are cheap but make many mistakes, while slow deliberation (a rat pausing at a maze fork, a crow planning tool use, a swarm of bees choosing a nest, an AI model writing thousands of hidden reasoning tokens) cuts mistakes but costs time and energy. It writes down a formula in which accuracy grows with the logarithm of thinking time, multiplies power by time to get the energy of each decision, and compares energy per resolved bit across animals and GPU clusters. It then claims to fit one 'Pareto surface' linking error, latency and power across 950 catalog systems and 25 hardware substrates. Almost every number in the paper turns out to be either typed into the text or hard-coded in the figure script rather than computed from the project's data files.

claims.claim: One AI reasoning run of 8,192 hidden tokens on 8 H100 GPUs uses a certain amount of electrical energy.
claims.paper_value: 5.6 kW for 120 s = 6.72×10⁵ J (82 J per token)
claims.data_value: 8 × 700 W (H100 power in the hardware file) = 5.6 kW; × 120 s = 6.72×10⁵ J; ÷ 8,192 = 82.0 J per token
claims.source: cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv (H100 power 700 W) plus the paper's own 120 s and 8,192 tokens
claims.note: I multiplied 5,600 W by 120 s and divided by 8,192 tokens; the arithmetic is right, but the same run is given as 6.30×10⁵ J (14 kW × 45 s) in section 2.4.3 and 3.0×10⁶ J (25 kW × 120 s) in the section 3 table, so the paper itself does not agree on this number.

claims.claim: An AI reasoning run dissipates vastly more energy than a human thinking about the same kind of problem.
claims.paper_value: five orders of magnitude (about 100,000 times), and in the next sentence 56-fold
claims.data_value: 6.72×10⁵ J ÷ 1.2×10⁴ J = 56 times, which is 1.7 orders of magnitude, not five
claims.source: Arithmetic on the paper's own numbers (20 W × 600 s = 12,000 J for the human; 5.6 kW × 120 s for the AI)
claims.note: I recomputed both ratios: 56 is correct for the numbers given, but '56-fold' and 'five orders of magnitude' describe the same gap and differ by a factor of about 1,800; the comparison also pits 120 s of AI against 600 s of human thinking, so it is not like-for-like.

claims.claim: The AI cluster spends far more energy per resolved bit of uncertainty than a human brain or a rat hippocampus.
claims.paper_value: 1.26×10⁵ J per bit; nearly 500 times the human brain; 8.4×10⁶ times the rat
claims.data_value: not in the data (bits resolved are assumed, not measured); arithmetic gives 14,000 W × 45 s = 6.30×10⁵ J ÷ 5 bits = 1.26×10⁵ J/bit; ÷ 266.7 J/bit (human) = 472 times; ÷ 0.015 J/bit (rat) = 8.4×10⁶ times
claims.source: Arithmetic only; no project file records bits resolved or deliberation power for these systems
claims.note: I recomputed all five energy-per-bit values and both ratios and they follow from the stated inputs, but the inputs (5.0 bits, 4.5 bits, 14 kW for 8 GPUs) are assumptions, and the paper's own marginal-cost formula would give a different number than the simple average it actually reports.

claims.claim: The human brain running at 20 W spends a tiny amount of energy per synaptic operation.
claims.data_value: 20 W ÷ 1.5×10¹⁴ operations per second = 1.33×10⁻¹³ J = 0.133 pJ (neural timeseries); but the hardware file lists a cortical synapse at 1×10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.01 pJ, 13 times lower
claims.source: neural_sensory_evolution_timeseries.csv (human brain row: 20 W, 1.5×10¹⁴ ops/s); cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv (cortical synapse row)
claims.note: I divided the brain power by the brain's operation rate in the timeseries file and got exactly 0.133 pJ, though the project's two data files disagree with each other by a factor of 13 on this quantity.

claims.claim: A rat deliberating at a maze fork uses a small, measurable amount of energy and climbs from near-chance to high accuracy.
claims.paper_value: 0.015 W for 0.85 s = 0.0128 J; accuracy 0.52 to 0.91 with fit coefficient 0.178 and R² = 0.94
claims.data_value: rat brain row: 0.12 W and 3.5 s deliberation, giving 0.42 J (33 times more); no accuracy or fit data anywhere in the project
claims.source: neural_sensory_evolution_timeseries.csv (brown rat row); catalog Systems sheet
claims.note: I multiplied the data file's rat brain power by its deliberation time and got 0.42 J versus the paper's 0.0128 J; the paper may mean only the hippocampus, but no file gives that, and the catalog id the paper cites for the rat resolves to a raven-and-wolf foraging partnership, not a rat.

claims.claim: A New Caledonian crow pausing before a multi-step tool puzzle spends a certain energy and jumps from 18% to 84% success.
claims.paper_value: 0.18 W for 8.0 s = 1.44 J; fit coefficient 0.241, R² = 0.91
claims.data_value: crow brain row: 1.8 W and 12 s deliberation, giving 21.6 J (15 times more); no success-rate data in the project
claims.note: I recomputed power × time from the project's crow row and got 21.6 J, ten times the paper's power and 15 times its energy; the 18% and 84% figures appear only in the text, and the catalog id cited for the crow resolves to the extinct small-bodied human Homo floresiensis.

claims.claim: A honeybee swarm choosing a nest site over four hours spends a certain energy and resolves about 3 bits.
claims.data_value: honeybee swarm row: collective power 20 W; × 14,400 s = 2.88×10⁵ J, 44 times more
claims.note: I multiplied the project's swarm power (20 W) by the paper's four hours and got 2.88×10⁵ J versus 6,480 J; the catalog id the paper cites for the bee swarm resolves to the lamprey's basal ganglia.

claims.claim: One Pareto surface relating error, latency and power fits 25 calibrated biological and digital substrates.
claims.paper_value: latency exponent 0.428 ± 0.035, power exponent 0.312 ± 0.041, R² = 0.884, N = 25, p < 10⁻¹²
claims.data_value: the hardware file has 33 rows and no error column at all, so the fit cannot be run; fitting the surface to the 10 points hard-coded in the figure script gives exponents 0.09 and 0.03 with R² 0.89; and with N = 25 and R² = 0.884 the smallest possible p is about 5×10⁻¹¹
claims.source: cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv (33 rows, columns for latency, power and energy per operation but none for error); scripts/generate_paper3_figures.py
claims.note: I checked the file (33 substrates, no error-rate column), tried the fit on the only error numbers in the project (the ten points typed into the figure script) and got completely different exponents, and ran an F-test showing the stated p-value is impossible for the stated N and R².

claims.claim: A blowfly's gyroscopic reflex takes about 5 ms at a tiny power and energy.
claims.data_value: 4.67×10⁻³ s, 5×10⁻⁴ W, 2.3×10⁻⁶ J (5 times the power, 4.6 times the energy)
claims.note: I read the blowfly row of the hardware file and checked that its power × latency equals its listed energy; the paper's table uses a power and energy about five times lower than the project's own entry.

claims.claim: The catalog behind the paper has a stated size.
claims.paper_value: 950 systems, 2,616 measurements across 2,624 observation ids, 1,275 sources, 64 sub-epochs; 25 hardware architectures
claims.data_value: 975 systems, 2,641 observation ids, 1,300 sources, 64 sub-epochs; 33 hardware rows
claims.source: Systema_Intelligentiae_Catalog.xlsx (Systems, Measurements, Sources, Planetary sheets); cleaned_hardware_benchmarks.csv
claims.note: I counted ids in each sheet; only the 64 sub-epochs match, every other count is 25 lower than the file, and the internal review file quotes a third set of counts (670 systems, 1,055 sources, 2,073 observations).

rationale.step: Reflexes are fast and cheap but make many mistakes on new situations; deliberation is slow and costly but more accurate.
rationale.note: The idea is reasonable, but the paper's own text says the blowfly reflex errs under 2% of the time while its figure plots the same reflex at 45% error, and no error-rate data exists in the project to settle it.

rationale.step: Error falls by a fixed mathematical law as thinking steps increase, and energy is power × time, so squeezing out the last errors costs exponentially more energy.
rationale.note: The paper uses four different laws for error versus thinking (exponential in section 2.2, logarithmic gain in 2.4.2, power law in 4, stretched exponential in 5), and its claim that steps must grow exponentially contradicts its own exponential-decay equation, under which steps grow only logarithmically.

rationale.step: The same logarithmic gain law, with similar coefficients, fits rats, crows, bee swarms and AI reasoning models.
rationale.note: No accuracy-versus-time data exists in the project for any of the four, the fits and R² values are typed into the text, the catalog ids cited for rat, crow, bee and human point to other organisms, and for the AI case the stated coefficients give an accuracy gain of 1.29, more than 100 percentage points.

rationale.step: AI deliberation costs enormously more energy per decision than biological deliberation, because GPUs shuttle weights between memory and compute while neurons store weights where they compute.
rationale.note: The direction is plausible and the 150 to 200 pJ per byte of memory traffic matches the hardware file's memory-bound H100 row (200 pJ), but the size of the gap is stated as 56 times, about 500 times and 100,000 times in different places, and the power of the same 8-GPU box is given as 5.6 kW, 14 kW and 25 kW.

rationale.step: All of this lies on one universal Pareto surface fitted across the catalog.
rationale.note: The data file the fit supposedly uses has no error column, the figure draws a hand-chosen curve rather than a fit, and six of the ten plotted systems sit inside the zone the paper calls forbidden.

conclusions.conclusion: Test-time reasoning in AI is the physical rediscovery of biological deliberation, obeying the same law.
conclusions.note: Nothing in the project data tests this; the four 'fits' exist only as sentences, and the analogy between reasoning tokens and hippocampal replay is asserted rather than measured.

conclusions.conclusion: Digital AI pays a huge energy toll per decision compared with brains, so future hardware must co-locate memory and compute.
conclusions.note: The hardware file does show a GPU memory fetch at 2×10⁻¹⁰ J against a synapse at 10⁻¹⁴ J (20,000 times), and 8 GPUs for two minutes really is around 10⁵ to 10⁶ J, so the direction holds, but the paper's own magnitudes contradict each other by factors of 4 to 1,800.

conclusions.conclusion: A universal speed-accuracy-energy Pareto surface with exponents 0.428 and 0.312 governs all 950 systems.
conclusions.note: The fit cannot be reproduced from any project file, its p-value is impossible for the stated sample size, and the figure's points violate the surface.

conclusions.conclusion: Brains route 99% of inputs through cheap reflexes and reserve deliberation for novel, high-stakes moments, and AI should copy this.
conclusions.note: The 99% figure has no source or data behind it anywhere in the manuscript or the project.

inconsistencies: The energy of one AI reasoning run is 6.72×10⁵ J in section 4.2 (5.6 kW × 120 s), 6.30×10⁵ J in section 2.4.3 (14 kW × 45 s) and 3.0×10⁶ J in the section 3 table (25 kW × 120 s); the same 8-GPU H100 box is given as 5.6 kW in one place and 14 kW in another.
Section 4.2 calls the brain-versus-AI energy gap 'five orders of magnitude' and, two sentences later, '56-fold'; the paper's own numbers give 56 (about 1.7 orders of magnitude).

The header and abstract say 950 systems, 2,616 measurements, 2,624 observation ids and 1,275 sources; the catalog file holds 975 systems, 2,641 observation ids and 1,300 sources, and the internal review file says 670 systems, 1,055 sources and 2,073 observations.
The paper says the hardware file holds 25 calibrated architectures and fits N = 25; the file has 33 rows and no error-rate column, so the section 5 fit could not have been run on it.

The catalog ids the paper attaches to its flagship systems resolve to different things in the catalog: the 'rat hippocampus' id is a raven-and-wolf foraging partnership, the 'crow' id is Homo floresiensis, the 'honeybee swarm' id is the lamprey basal ganglia, the 'human neocortex' id is the sea-slug gill-withdrawal reflex, the 'blowfly' id is the fruit-fly connectome, and the 'mantis shrimp' id is a snapping shrimp (a different animal); the frontier-AI id is a 100,000-GPU cluster drawing 1.2×10⁸ W in the timeseries file, not an 8-GPU box.

Of the 28 footnotes, only one (Bartol et al. 2015) carries a catalog source id that actually points to that paper; the other 27 ids point to unrelated works, and several cited papers (Landauer 1961, Redish 2016, Snell et al. 2024, Hoffmann et al. 2022, Friston 2010, Kahneman 2011) are not in the source registry at all.

The rat's final error is 9% in section 2.4.2 (accuracy 0.91), under 5% in section 3.2 and 5% in Figure 1; the number of sweeps is 4 to 12 in section 2.4.2 and 4 to 8 in the table; section 2.4.2 attributes the sweeps to theta rhythm while section 3.2 and the table attribute them to sharp-wave ripples.

The deliberation gain law applied to the AI case with the stated coefficient (0.214) and time constant (1.8 s) over 750 s gives a gain of 1.29, which is impossible if accuracy is a fraction between 0 and 1 as it is for the rat and crow examples.

The symbol alpha means a gain coefficient of 0.18 to 0.27 in section 2.4.2 and a latency exponent of 0.428 in section 5; the energy-per-bit formula in 2.4.3 is a marginal cost but every number under it is a plain average (energy divided by bits).

Figure 1 draws the 'Pareto boundary' from a hand-typed formula (0.5 × exp(−1.5 × t^0.4) + 0.005), not from a fit, its exponent 0.4 is not the paper's 0.428, it has no power term, and six of the ten plotted systems (mantis shrimp, Mauthner escape, human saccade, rat, AlphaZero and more) lie below it, inside the zone the text calls forbidden.
Figure 2 is a hard-coded power law (exponent 0.52) that gives 4.8% error at 8,192 tokens and 9.9% at 2,048 tokens, while Figure 1 plots the same two systems at 0.8% and 2% error.
Figure 3 bar values disagree with the hardware file: SpiNNaker 2 at 8.3×10⁹ versus 6.67×10¹¹ operations per joule, NorthPole 2.0×10¹² versus 2.5×10¹², B200 1.2×10¹³ versus 4.5×10¹².

Section 3.1 says the blowfly reflex errs under 2% of the time on predictable gusts, yet Figure 1 plots it at 45% error; the table's blowfly power (0.0001 W) is five times lower than the project's own blowfly row (0.0005 W).
The manuscript never refers to any of its three figures in the text.
bottom_line: A careful reader can rely on the simple arithmetic (power × time gives the stated joules, 5.6 kW for 120 s is 6.72×10⁵ J, and GPUs really do spend thousands of times more energy per operation than synapses in the project's hardware file). Nothing else is checkable: the animal and AI deliberation fits, the universal Pareto surface, the energy-per-bit ratios and the figures are typed-in numbers that contradict each other and the project's data, and the catalog ids point to the wrong organisms.
